q: Which of these take up space in **flash**, the non-volatile program memory? Select all that apply.
code:
const uint16_t sine_table[256] = { /* ... */ };   /* A */
int retries = 3;                                   /* B */
static uint8_t rx_buf[512];                        /* C */
void loop(void) { char line[80]; /* ... */ }      /* D */
explain: Code (`.text`) and constants (`.rodata`) live in flash. **Initialised globals** (`.data`) need RAM at runtime *and* a copy of their initial value in flash, which the startup code copies across before `main`. `.bss` is only zeroed at boot, so it needs no flash, just RAM. Locals live on the stack, in RAM, only while the function runs.

q: A logger has run for 3 weeks with mixed-size `malloc`/`free`. The heap stats say **6 KB free**, yet `malloc(2048)` returns NULL. What's going on?
options: Fragmentation: the free memory is split into many small holes, and none of them is 2 KB long
A memory leak: the 6 KB figure is wrong
`malloc` can't allocate more than 1 KB on a microcontroller
The stack has grown into the heap
explain: Free space isn't the same as *contiguous* free space. After many mixed-size allocs and frees, the heap is full of small gaps. It passes a 10-minute test and fails in the field. A fixed-block pool makes this impossible, because every hole is exactly one block. A leak would show *less* free memory, not unusable free memory. A stack collision is a different (and worse) failure that usually corrupts data rather than returning NULL.

q: A task has a **1024-byte** stack. Its recursive `parse()` function has a local `uint8_t tmp[240]`, plus 32 bytes of saved registers and return address per call (272 bytes per frame). Ignoring everything else, how many nested calls fit **completely** before the stack overflows?
explain: 1024 / 272 = 3.76, so 3 frames fit (816 bytes) and the 4th one runs off the end. On a Cortex-M with no MPU, the 4th call doesn't crash. It silently overwrites whatever sits below the stack (often `.bss` or another task's stack). That's why safety standards ban unbounded recursion and why you measure stack high-water marks.

q: Why does a fixed-block pool make your firmware **more predictable** than a general-purpose `malloc`?
options: Alloc and free are O(1) pops and pushes on a free list, and because all blocks are the same size, fragmentation can't happen
It uses less RAM than `malloc` for any workload
Pools never run out of memory
explain: Constant-time operations give you a **bounded** worst-case execution time, and equal-sized blocks mean any free block satisfies any request. Pools *can* waste RAM, because a 10-byte object in a 32-byte block wastes 22. They *do* run out, but at a known count you can size for and test. They aren't magically thread-safe either: a pool shared with an ISR still needs a critical section around its free list.
